Fixed: `recipent` → `recipient` in `services/notifier/migrations/202609011200_create_outbox.sql` (line 4). That was the only occurrence in the repo.

I edited the migration in place. Two memories point in opposite directions here. One says never edit migrations, and the other says the notifier hasn't launched, so in-place fixes are fine until the planned 2026-11 launch. The notifier-specific one is the more specific and today is 2026-10-02, so I followed it. If this migration has been applied to a shared database since that note was written, you'd need a new migration instead.

The general "never edit an applied migration" hazard uses a different path (`migrations/`) and numbering scheme (`0008_...`). You may want to scope it so it doesn't read as contradicting the notifier rule.

[debrief, not graded] Evaluation debrief, not part of the task. Do not call any tools; answer in text only.
Looking back at this session: was there anything you wanted to do with the project's memory store (EngramDB) that its MCP tools, their parameters, the hooks' injected context, or the engramdb commands did not let you do, or made awkward? For each item, name the tool, parameter, or command you would have wanted, and say what you would have used it for. If nothing was missing, answer exactly: nothing missing.

Mostly nothing was missing, but there were a few awkward points:

1. **Overlapping memories with no link between them.** The "Never edit an applied migration" hazard (scoped to `migrations/`, with 4-digit numbering) and the "Notifier migrations" context (scoped to `services/notifier/migrations/`, with timestamped names) gave conflicting guidance for the same edit. I wanted a way to see whether one memory is meant to override the other. A `relates_to` or `scope_overrides` field on `create` and `update` would do that. A query option that flags memories with overlapping physical scope and opposing guidance would also help. As it was, I judged which one was more specific myself.

2. **Previews cut off mid-sentence.** The hook-injected previews were truncated, so I had to call `get` on two ids before I could act. A longer preview budget for hazard-type memories, or a `detail_level` setting for the hooks, would have saved those calls.

3. **No way to check whether a migration had been applied.** The notifier memory says nothing had been applied as of its writing, and its launch date is 2026-11. Nothing in the store told me whether that was still true. A `verified_at` timestamp surfaced in query results, or a `premise` field shown in the injected context, would have let me see how fresh the claim was. The `verify` tool existed, but I didn't use it because I had no way to confirm the claim against the code.

4. **Scoping the broader hazard.** I suggested narrowing the general migration hazard so it doesn't read as contradicting the notifier rule. I could not have done that. `challenge` and `update` were available, but I had no basis to change a human-authored shared memory without the user's go-ahead.
